title: The garden and the one tree
hookLine: Adam and his wife live in the garden with everything, told only to leave one tree (2:35)
last: IBLIS — PRIDE WAS THE FIRST MISTAKE.

lines: A FRIEND'S APARTMENT FOR A MONTH.
cards: A friend lends you their apartment for a month. The fridge is full. Use the car, the pool, the good coffee, the books.
Honestly, anything. Just one thing: don't open that cupboard in the hall. A hundred yeses and a single no, and it's an old joke which one ends up on people's minds that first night.
Now Adam gets a home: a garden with everything in it. And one rule.

teach.h: BUT COME NOT NIGH THIS TREE.
teach.b: God says: Adam, live in the garden, you and your wife, and in Pickthall's words, “eat ye freely (of the fruits) thereof where ye will; but come not nigh this tree lest ye become wrongdoers.” Freely, where you will.
The permission is huge, and it comes first. Another surah describes the garden's promise: no hunger there, no nakedness, no thirst, no burning sun. Then the one tree.
Not even don't eat, exactly: don't come near it. Keep your distance. Here's what the Qur'an doesn't say.

It doesn't name Adam's wife; the name Hawwa, Eve, comes from the hadith and later tradition. It doesn't name the tree, or the fruit. There's no apple in the Qur'an; the apple came later, from outside it.
Commentators guessed at wheat, or grapes, or figs, and al-Tabari concluded that we simply aren't told.
Scholars even differ about the garden itself: some say it was the paradise of the hereafter, others a garden somewhere on earth.
The Qur'an leaves these open and keeps its eye on one thing: a whole world of yes, and a single no. Why a no at all?

teach.h: A LIMIT MAKES IT A TRUST.
teach.b: One answer some scholars give: a steward, a khalifah, has to be someone who can be trusted with a limit.
A life with no limits isn't a trust; it's a playground. The one tree turns the garden into a test of love, and of trust.

how: Muslims read the garden story in surahs two, seven and twenty; teachers often draw from it that the permitted, halal, is wide and the forbidden is narrow.

o: a steward who can be trusted with a limit
the angel set to guard the forbidden tree
the garden's owner, free to take anything

games.q: what's inside the garden — tap the pairs.
p: keep your distance from one tree
Eve: named in hadith and tradition

s: the Qur'an says the forbidden fruit was an apple
it never names the fruit or the tree. the apple came later, from outside the Qur'an.
it calls her his wife. the name Hawwa, Eve, comes from hadith and later tradition.
the rule was to not even come near the tree
"come not nigh this tree": keep your distance.

games.q: you've been given a garden with everything in it. eat freely, anywhere. one tree, don't go near. what's the first thing the story tells you?
o: that you may eat freely, where you will.
what will happen if you disobey.
games.why: the permission comes first, and it's huge: eat freely, where you will. the no is a single tree.

practice: Make a quiet list of what you already have enough of: light to see by, air in this breath, a bed, something to eat later, someone who'd answer if you called.

Let it get long, and notice how big the garden already is; if your mind drifts to the one thing you don't have, see it and come back to the list. If you pray, close it with alhamdulillah for the garden.

wordCard.voice: Khalifah, a steward trusted with one limit: a garden of everything given freely, where you will, except a single place not to go near.

orig.note: Arabic: "this tree," the words of 2:35. shajarah is the ordinary word for a tree.

carryVoice: Your line: everything, minus one. The yes comes first, and it is far bigger than the no. Twenty-five days in.
